title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Introductory Microbiology — 2024
subject: biology
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: What are the characteristic features of bacteria? Give one example each of beneficial and harmful bacteria.
questions.solution:
**Bacteria (Monera):** prokaryotic, unicellular, no true nucleus, peptidoglycan wall, binary fission.

Beneficial: *Rhizobium* (nitrogen fixation), *Lactobacillus* (curd). Harmful: *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* (TB), *Salmonella typhi* (typhoid).
questions.knowledgeNote: Shapes: cocci (spheres), bacilli (rods), spirilla (spirals) — shape vocabulary recurs in one-markers.
questions.answer: **Characteristic features of bacteria:** prokaryotic unicellular microbes — no true nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; peptidoglycan cell wall; shapes cocci/bacilli/spirilla/vibrio; may carry flagella, pili, plasmids; reproduce by binary fission; nutrition autotrophic or heterotrophic; some form endospores. **Beneficial:** ***Lactobacillus*** (curd formation) — or Rhizobium (N-fixation). **Harmful:** ***Vibrio cholerae*** (cholera) — or *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* (TB). **Deep point:** one body plan, every metabolism — bacteria run the biosphere's recycling and our infections with the same cellular simplicity.

questions.question: Why are viruses considered to be on the borderline between living and non-living? Give reasons.
questions.solution:
**Living traits:** carry genetic material (DNA/RNA), mutate and evolve, multiply inside hosts.

**Non-living traits:** no cell, no metabolism, no response to stimuli; crystallisable like chemicals (Stanley, TMV).

Hence the borderline — alive only inside a host cell.
questions.knowledgeNote: Viruses are obligate parasites: zero independent metabolism, which is why antibiotics cannot touch them.
questions.answer: **Viruses on the borderline of living and non-living:** **Living-like characters:** they contain **genetic material (DNA or RNA)**, they **replicate** (inside a host), they show **mutation and evolution**, and they are host-specific and infectious. **Non-living characters:** they are **acellular** — no cell membrane, cytoplasm or organelles; they have **no metabolism of their own** (no enzymes for energy generation); they can be **crystallised and stored like chemicals**, and the crystallised virus shows **no sign of life** until it enters a host. **Conclusion:** a virus is an **obligate intracellular parasite** — a packet of genetic information that is inert outside a cell and alive only in the sense of being replicated inside one. **Deep point:** the virus forces the definition of life to include 'self-sustaining metabolism' — a virus has heredity but not metabolism, which is why it sits exactly on the boundary.

questions.question: Describe the lytic cycle of a bacteriophage with a diagram description.
questions.solution: (1) **Attachment:** tail fibres grip the bacterial wall. (2) **Penetration:** DNA injected, capsid outside. (3) **Biosynthesis:** host machinery hijacked to make viral DNA and proteins. (4) **Maturation:** new phages assembled. (5) **Lysis:** lysozyme bursts the cell, ~100–200 virions released.
questions.knowledgeNote: Lytic (kill now) vs lysogenic (prophage sleeps) — the two viral lifestyles behind one more comparison question.
questions.answer: **Lytic cycle of a T-even bacteriophage:** **(1) Attachment (adsorption):** tail fibres recognise and bind to specific receptors on the host bacterium's cell wall. **(2) Penetration:** the base plate settles on the wall, the **tail sheath contracts**, and the needle-like core pierces the wall; the **phage DNA is injected** into the cytoplasm — the empty protein capsid remains outside as a 'ghost'. **(3) Biosynthesis:** phage DNA commandeers the host's RNA polymerase, ribosomes and metabolism; bacterial DNA, RNA and protein synthesis are shut down; **phage mRNA → phage proteins (capsid, sheath, lysozyme) and phage DNA copies** are produced. **(4) Maturation (assembly):** DNA heads are packaged, tails and tail fibres attach — hundreds of complete virions assemble inside the cell. **(5) Lysis and release:** phage-encoded **lysozyme digests the bacterial cell wall**; the cell bursts (lyses), releasing ~100–200 progeny phages, each free to infect a new cell (whole cycle ≈ 25 min). **Diagram description:** bacterium (oval) with phage on surface (head + tail + fibres) → DNA entering → cell filled with viral parts → cell bursting with new phages escaping. **Deep point:** the lytic cycle is a hijacking timetable — attach, inject, reprogram, assemble, burst; the 'lytic' name records its last act, and its alternative (the lysogenic cycle) keeps the phage DNA quietly inserted instead.

questions.question: What is Gram staining? Distinguish between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
questions.solution:
**Gram staining** (Christian Gram) separates bacteria by wall structure: crystal violet → iodine → alcohol wash → safranin counterstain.

**Gram-positive:** thick peptidoglycan retains violet (e.g. *Staphylococcus*). **Gram-negative:** thin wall, outer membrane — violet washes out, stains pink (e.g. *E. coli*).
questions.knowledgeNote: The stain predicts antibiotics: penicillin hits Gram-positive walls; Gram-negative outer membranes resist it.
questions.answer: **Gram staining:** a differential staining technique (Christian Gram, 1884) that divides bacteria into two groups by their **cell-wall structure** — crystal violet → iodine (mordant, fixes the dye) → alcohol/acetone decolourisation → safranin (counterstain). **Gram-positive bacteria:** retain the **crystal violet–iodine complex** even after alcohol (thick peptidoglycan layer traps the complex) — appear **purple/violet**; e.g. *Staphylococcus*, *Streptococcus*, *Bacillus*. **Gram-negative bacteria:** the complex **washes out** in alcohol (thin peptidoglycan plus an outer lipopolysaccharide membrane dissolves in the decolouriser) — take up the counterstain and appear **pink/red**; e.g. *E. coli*, *Salmonella*, *Vibrio*. **Deep point:** the colour difference is a cell-wall thickness test — the alcohol step is the discriminator, and the result guides antibiotic choice (Gram-positive walls are the target of penicillin; Gram-negative outer membranes confer extra resistance).

questions.question: What are cyanobacteria? Explain their role in nitrogen fixation with an example.
questions.solution:
**Cyanobacteria** (blue-green algae) are photosynthetic prokaryotes — the first oxygen producers.

Heterocyst-forming types (*Nostoc, Anabaena*) fix atmospheric N₂ via nitrogenase in low-oxygen heterocysts, enriching paddy fields — the original biofertiliser of Asian rice farming.
questions.knowledgeNote: Azolla–Anabaena symbiosis in paddies fixes ~30–60 kg N/ha free — traditional farming's nitrogen factory.
questions.answer: **Cyanobacteria:** photosynthetic, **prokaryotic** microorganisms formerly called 'blue-green algae' — they contain **chlorophyll a** and perform oxygenic photosynthesis, have peptidoglycan walls, occur in chains/filaments (e.g. *Nostoc*, *Anabaena*, *Oscillatoria*), and many fix nitrogen in specialised thick-walled cells called **heterocysts** (where nitrogenase works in an oxygen-free environment). **Role in nitrogen fixation:** inside heterocysts, cyanobacteria convert atmospheric **N₂ → NH₃ (ammonia)** using the enzyme nitrogenase, enriching soil and water with usable nitrogen — a major natural input to the nitrogen cycle. **Example:** ***Nostoc*** colonies in rice paddies and wet fields fix nitrogen and serve as a biofertiliser, reducing the need for nitrogenous fertiliser; *Anabaena* forms a symbiosis with the water fern *Azolla* in rice fields. **Deep point:** the heterocyst is the solution to a biochemical contradiction — nitrogenase is destroyed by oxygen, so the cyanobacterium builds a dedicated, oxygen-free chamber for nitrogen fixation while its other cells keep photosynthesising.

questions.question: Write any four economic importances of microbes.
questions.solution: (1) Dairy: *Lactobacillus* curd/cheese. (2) Medicine: *Penicillium* antibiotics, yeast insulin. (3) Biogas/bioremediation: methanogens digest waste. (4) Agriculture: *Rhizobium* biofertiliser; (5) industry: yeast brewing, *Aspergillus* citric acid.
questions.knowledgeNote: One beneficial + one harmful example per group is the safest answering pattern for 'importance' questions.
questions.answer: **Four economic importances of microbes:** (1) **Food and fermentation** — *Lactobacillus* in curd, yeast in bread and alcohol, fungi in cheese; (2) **agriculture** — nitrogen-fixing *Rhizobium* and *Nostoc* as biofertilisers; composting and biogas production; (3) **medicine and industry** — antibiotics (penicillin from *Penicillium*), vaccines, vitamins, enzymes, sewage treatment; (4) **harmful roles** — diseases (cholera, TB, malaria's Plasmodium), food spoilage and crop diseases — knowing the harm is as economically important as the benefit. **Deep point:** microbes are the biosphere's chemical industry — every fermentation tank, sewage plant and compost heap is a managed microbial population.
